transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I’m just worrying all the time. My mind keeps jumping from one thing to the next—like whether the new partnership at our lab is going to mean my position gets cut, or whether my data is wrong, or if my bills are going to start piling up. Then I start thinking my family probably sees me as falling behind, and that I’ve already ruined my chances at grad school. It’s constant, and it’s getting hard to handle.
Have you been avoiding any activities or situations because of your worries?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’m avoiding anything obvious on purpose. I still go to work and deal with stuff. Maybe I put things off sometimes when I’m worried, but I haven’t really thought of it as avoiding specific situations.
Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms like headaches or difficulty sleeping?

Yeah. Mostly it’s tension. My shoulders and neck are tight pretty much all day, and I notice I’m clenching my jaw when I’m working through spreadsheets. By the evening I’ll get headaches and feel stiff, like I’ve been carrying heavy equipment around all day.
Has something very stressful or traumatic happened to you recently?

Not traumatic exactly, but it’s been really stressful. It started about seven months ago, when the lab’s funding shifted and this commercial partnership changed how everything was being run. That’s when the worrying really picked up.
Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time lately?
I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve been stressed and worn out, but I wouldn’t say I feel sad or down most of the time.
Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind and feel like you can't control them?

Yeah, that happens a lot. I’ll try to make myself focus on one thing, like finishing a report or checking an assay, but then one worry turns into another. Pretty soon I’m just staring at the screen, and my mind is running through every possible way things could go wrong.
Do you feel like these repeating thoughts are irrational or unrealistic?

Some of them probably are unrealistic, yeah. Like, I know one bad result doesn’t automatically mean all my data is wrong, or that I’ve ruined my chances at grad school. But in the moment it feels real. My mind just keeps jumping from getting cut from the lab, to bills piling up, to my family thinking I’m falling behind, and I can’t really shut it off.
Do you feel compelled to perform specific rituals or behaviors to reduce your anxiety?
I don’t think so. I mean, I’ll check things sometimes if I’m worried, but I don’t have like a specific ritual I feel I have to do to make the anxiety go away.
Do you worry about being judged or evaluated by others?

Yeah, I do. I worry a lot about what people think, especially at work and with my family. Like, I’ll start thinking the lab’s new partnership might mean my position gets cut, or that my data is wrong and people will see me as incompetent. Then it turns into worrying my bills will pile up, my family thinks I’m falling behind, and that I’ve already messed up my chances at grad school. It’s hard to stop once it starts.
Do you feel like these thoughts are intrusive, meaning they come into your mind even when you don't want them to?

Yeah, they do. I’ll try to tell myself, like, just focus on this one thing—finish the report or check the assay—but then one worry triggers another. Pretty soon I’m just staring at the screen, and my head is running through every possible way things could go wrong.
Do you feel like you have to repeat certain actions or mental acts in response to your worries?

No, not really. I don’t feel like I have to repeat actions or count things or say things in my head a certain way. I just get stuck worrying, but I’m not doing some specific thing over and over to deal with it.
Do you feel like these worries are taking over your mind and you can't think about anything else?

Yeah, it really can feel like that. I’ll try to make myself focus on one thing, like finishing a report or checking an assay, but then one worry leads into another. After a while I’m just staring at the screen and my mind is running through every possible thing that could go wrong.
Are your worries affecting your relationships with family or friends?

Yeah, it is. I’ve been dropping the ball on stuff, and that affects people around me. I missed an internal lab deadline because I couldn’t get my writing and data review organized, and then outside of work, even normal things feel hard to keep up with. Like showing up for art nights with friends, or cooking for my family—stuff I should be able to do just feels like too much sometimes.
Are you finding it harder to enjoy things you used to like doing because of your worries?

Yeah. It’s harder to enjoy them because they start feeling like responsibilities I’m failing at. I used to like art nights with friends, and cooking for my family was something I could just do, but now I’m worrying so much and falling behind on things that even that feels like too much to keep up with. Even at work, I missed an internal lab deadline because I couldn’t get my writing and data review organized, and it kind of spills over into everything.
Do you feel like you have unwanted thoughts that are disturbing or inappropriate and keep repeating in your mind?
I don’t think so. I mean, I have thoughts that repeat, but they’re more worries about things going wrong or stuff I need to fix. They don’t feel disturbing or inappropriate in that way.
How long have you been experiencing these worries?
It’s been about seven months now. It started around when the lab’s funding shifted and the commercial partnership changed how everything was being run.
Have you noticed any significant impact on your daily life or relationships due to your constant worrying?

Yes, definitely. It’s affecting day-to-day stuff a lot. I missed an internal deadline at the lab because I just couldn’t get my writing and data review organized, and since then it feels like even normal responsibilities are piling up. Preparing reports feels overwhelming, and outside of work I’m not keeping up well either — like getting to art nights or cooking for my family feels like too much sometimes.
Do you feel like your worrying is interfering with your ability to function at work or in your personal life?

Yes. It’s definitely getting in the way. At work, I missed an internal lab deadline because I couldn’t get my writing and data review organized. And now even normal things feel hard to keep up with, like preparing reports. Outside of work too — I’ve been missing art nights, and even cooking for my family feels like too much sometimes.
Do you think your worrying would stop or significantly decrease if the situation at your lab and with the commercial partnership were to resolve favorably?

I don’t think it would fully stop, no. It might help with one part of it, but my mind keeps jumping to other things too — like whether my data is wrong, whether my bills are going to pile up, whether my family thinks I’m falling behind, or if I’ve already messed up my chances at grad school. So even if the lab situation worked out, I think the worrying would just move somewhere else.
